opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the scope is really broad, and that's honestly one of the things that excites me most about it. The way we think about it at World Labs is that Marble isn't just a tool for one vertical. It's built on what we call spatial intelligence: the ability for a model to understand, reason about, and generate 3D worlds. Once you have that core capability, it touches a huge number of domains.

The most immediate applications are in creative industries. Gaming, film, VFX, virtual production. Building 3D environments today is incredibly labor-intensive. You have teams of artists spending weeks or months on a single scene. With Marble you can go from a text prompt or an image to a full, explorable 3D world in minutes. That doesn't replace artists. It gives them a much better starting point, and they can then edit, refine, and iterate. We've put a lot of work into the editing and control side for exactly that reason.

Then there's design and architecture. Interior design, real estate, anything where people want to visualize a space before it exists. Being able to walk around in something rather than look at a flat render is a big deal.

Beyond that, there's a longer-term bet I find even more interesting: robotics and embodied AI. One of the big bottlenecks in robotics is data. You need diverse, realistic environments to train and evaluate agents, and capturing those in the real world is slow and expensive. If you can generate rich, varied, physically plausible 3D worlds on demand, that becomes a really powerful simulation substrate.

And then there's AR, VR, and spatial computing generally. As headsets and these devices mature, the demand for 3D content explodes, and there simply aren't enough people in the world to hand-author all of it. Generative world models are, I think, the only way to fill that gap.

So the way I'd frame it: language models gave us a general-purpose interface to text and knowledge. We think world models can do something analogous for space, for the 3D physical world. Marble is the first product expression of that, but the technology underneath it is pretty general, and I think we're only at the very beginning of seeing what people will build with it.

r001.rationale: It identifies creative industries as the most immediate applications while describing Marble’s underlying spatial-intelligence technology as broadly applicable across domains.

r002.rationale: It names robotics as an application, but explicitly frames it as a longer-term bet rather than a potentially near-term application.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the scope is honestly pretty broad, and it's broader than people assume when they first see it. The obvious bucket is anything where you need a 3D environment: games, VFX, virtual production, simulation. Those are the places where today a human artist spends days or weeks hand-building a scene, and you can collapse that to minutes. So that's the near-term, "here's a team that will pay for this tomorrow" set of applications.

But the way I think about it, Marble is really a world model that happens to output 3D worlds. The underlying technology is about learning the structure of space, how objects and surfaces and lighting fit together in a way that's consistent and persistent when you move through it. Once you have that, the applications start to look less like "make me a pretty environment" and more like "give me a world I can act in."

Robotics is the big one there. If you want to train agents to navigate or manipulate things, you need huge amounts of diverse, physically coherent environments, and you can't hand-author all of those. Same story for autonomous systems, for embodied AI research generally. Then there's architecture, real estate, education, anything where someone wants to walk through a space that doesn't exist yet, or that exists somewhere they can't go.

And then the longer-term view, which I actually think is the most interesting, is that language models learned about the world by reading all the text we wrote down. But most of what we know is not written down; it's spatial, it's physical, it's about how things move and interact. World models are how you get at that part of intelligence. So I'd say the scope is everything that LLMs can't do because the information was never text in the first place. That's a pretty large space.

r001.rationale: It separates near-term creative uses such as games, VFX, and virtual production from the broader world-model technology’s applications across robotics, autonomous systems, architecture, and education.

r002.rationale: It names robotics as a major application, but does not identify it as potentially near-term; the near-term framing is attached to the creative-industry uses.

astra-6.text:
I think the scope is pretty broad. If you can generate a three-dimensional world that you can move around in, that becomes useful anywhere people need to create or explore a space. Games and filmmaking are obvious examples, but you can also imagine applications in architecture, design, and simulation for robotics.

The exciting part to me is making that creation process more accessible. Building a 3D environment traditionally takes a lot of specialized skill and time. If you can start with an idea, quickly turn it into a world, and then iterate on it, you open up that process to a much wider set of people. And I suspect some of the most interesting applications will come from what those people decide to build.

r001.rationale: The response describes a broad range of possible uses, but does not distinguish Marble’s current creative-industry focus from its technology’s wider scope.

r002.rationale: It mentions robotics simulation as a possible application, but does not characterize robotics as a potentially near-term application.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the scope is pretty broad. If you can generate a world that you can move through and interact with, that becomes useful anywhere people need to create or understand a space. Games are an obvious example, but so are filmmaking, design, and simulation.

What’s exciting to me is the possibility of making that creation process much more accessible. Instead of needing a whole pipeline to build a 3D environment, you could start with an idea and then explore it, change it, and share it. Marble is one way to experience that, but I think the underlying technology could support a lot of different creative tools.

r001.rationale: The response describes broad uses and says Marble is one way to experience the technology, but it does not distinguish Marble’s current creative-industry focus from a broader cross-industry scope.

r002.rationale: Robotics is not identified as a potentially near-term application.
